behavior_items: The reproducer targets C++20 constant-evaluation rules for class types with non-trivial destructors, specifically std::string.
The bug report claims that std::string's destructor is rejected as not being a constant expression in a case where the standard permits compile-time destruction.

The exercised compiler path is the constexpr evaluator for object lifetime: construct a std::string during constant evaluation, then verify that its destructor can also run during the same constant-evaluated context.
In C++20, the library expanded constexpr support for std::basic_string, so operations that create, modify, and destroy suitable std::string objects may be valid in constant expressions.

A typical reproducer for this issue is minimal because the failure is not about string algorithms themselves, but about whether the implementation marks and handles std::string destruction as constexpr-capable.

The relevant semantic sequence is: create a std::string in a constexpr context, possibly initialized from a short literal, let it go out of scope, and require the whole expression to remain a core constant expression.
This especially exercises the small-string case, where no dynamic allocation is required, because such objects are natural candidates for successful constant evaluation and destruction.

The compiler must evaluate not only the constructor and accessors of std::string, but also the cleanup phase at end of lifetime; the reported bug indicates GCC incorrectly rejects at that destruction step.

If GCC diagnoses that the destructor is not constexpr, it means either the library declaration, builtin constant-evaluation rules, or front-end checks for destructors are too restrictive for std::string in C++20 mode.

The reproducer therefore distinguishes between two behaviors: accepted constant evaluation when std::string fully participates in constexpr as required, versus erroneous rejection when the destructor is treated as non-constexpr.

The issue is specifically about language-library interaction: the core language allows constant destruction under C++20 rules, while libstdc++ and/or GCC front-end machinery must correctly expose std::string's destructor as usable in constexpr evaluation.

The failure is likely triggered by a compile-time assertion, constexpr variable initialization, or consteval/constexpr function return, any of which forces the compiler to prove that the temporary or local std::string can be destroyed during constant evaluation.
No runtime behavior is needed to expose the bug; a compile-only test is sufficient because the relevant behavior is acceptance or rejection of a constant-expression context.
The reproducer is effectively checking standards conformance for C++20 constexpr std::string support rather than testing ordinary string functionality.

Because the provided reproducer text matches the bug title rather than showing source code, the central exercised behavior can still be inferred: a minimal constexpr use of std::string that fails solely due to destructor handling.
test_behavior_analysis.summary: This reproducer exercises GCC's C++20 constant-expression handling for std::string object lifetime. The important logic is not complex string processing, but whether a std::string created in a constexpr-required context can also be destroyed there. Under C++20, std::basic_string gained constexpr support, so for valid cases—especially small-string cases without problematic allocation—the compiler should accept construction, use, and destruction during constant evaluation. The reported failure means GCC incorrectly treats std::string's destructor as not usable in a constant expression, causing a compile-time rejection where standard-conforming behavior is acceptance.

test_failure_analysis.analysis: The common pattern is a C++20 constexpr-evaluation failure centered on object lifetime completion rather than on string operations themselves. The reproducer conceptually creates a std::string in a constant-evaluated context, uses only simple/small-string behavior, and then fails when GCC checks whether end-of-scope destruction is allowed in a core constant expression. That points to a compiler/library integration bug in constexpr destruction handling for std::basic_string under C++20. The failure pattern strongly suggests GCC accepts or nearly accepts constexpr construction/use of std::string but rejects the cleanup phase, meaning the bug is likely in destructor constexpr eligibility checks, constant-evaluation lifetime modeling, or recognition of libstdc++'s constexpr annotations for std::string and its bases/members. Because the likely case is small-string optimization with no heap allocation, a rejection is unlikely to be caused by true dynamic-storage restrictions and more likely by over-conservative compiler logic that treats std::string's non-trivial destructor as inherently non-constexpr or fails to propagate C++20 constant-destruction rules through library types.
possible_causes: GCC front-end constexpr validation incorrectly rejects non-trivial destructors for class types in C++20 constant expressions, even when the destructor is permitted and the object's lifetime begins and ends within the same evaluation.
The constexpr evaluator mishandles end-of-lifetime cleanup for std::basic_string objects, treating destruction as a separate forbidden operation instead of a valid part of constant evaluation.
GCC may fail to recognize libstdc++'s std::basic_string destructor as constexpr-capable in C++20 mode due to missing or incorrectly interpreted declaration metadata during semantic checks.

There may be a bug in constant-expression checking for temporary/local variables with non-trivial destructors, where the compiler rejects them generically instead of examining whether the actual destructor body is valid for constexpr execution.

The evaluator may incorrectly model std::string internals used by small-string optimization, concluding that destruction touches forbidden state or non-constant storage even when no dynamic allocation occurred.

A defect may exist in GCC's language-library interaction for special member functions, where constexpr status of std::basic_string depends on base/member destructors and the compiler fails to propagate that status through the instantiated type.

GCC may be applying pre-C++20 restrictions on destructors or literal-type-like rules when checking std::string in constexpr contexts, causing an outdated conformance check to reject valid C++20 constant destruction.

The compiler could have a bug in core constant-expression diagnostics for cleanup actions, misattributing failure to the destructor itself when the real issue is incorrect bookkeeping of constructed objects and required destruction during constexpr evaluation.
evidence: The reported failure is specifically that std::string's destructor is considered not a constant expression when it should be.
The test behavior emphasizes that construction and simple use are not the interesting part; the rejection happens at the destruction step at end of lifetime.
C++20 explicitly expanded constexpr support for std::basic_string, so a small-string case should be a valid compile-time scenario.
The reproducer is compile-only and checks standards conformance of constant evaluation, which points to front-end constexpr semantics rather than runtime code generation.
The scenario likely uses a short literal/small-string optimization case, reducing the likelihood that real dynamic allocation constraints are the cause.
The bug description itself highlights language-library interaction, indicating either GCC constexpr machinery or recognition of libstdc++ declarations is too restrictive.

This file implements constexpr validation/evaluation logic, including checks for literal/constexpr suitability and likely the rules that could still be applying overly restrictive pre-C++20 destructor constraints to std::string.

Destruction is exercised through implicit/end-of-scope destructor calls, so C++ call-building and special-member invocation handling may be incorrectly determining that std::string's destructor is not constexpr-capable or not callable in a constant-expression context.

The reproducer likely fails during constexpr variable initialization or checking of a local/temporary object with non-trivial destruction. Declaration and initialization processing in the C++ frontend is a plausible place for rejecting such objects too early based on outdated literal-type or destructor rules.

std::string destructor constexpr eligibility depends on special member function properties and propagation through class machinery. If GCC mishandles destructor property computation for instantiated class types, this file is a plausible source.

End-of-scope cleanup and semantic handling of temporaries/locals in constexpr-required contexts may be modeled here. A bug in semantic bookkeeping for cleanup actions could manifest as incorrectly blaming the destructor.

gcc/cp/decl.cc.summary: We're initializing a local variable which has a cleanup GUARD. If there are any temporaries used in the initializer INIT of this variable, we need to wrap their cleanups with TRY_CATCH_EXPR (, GUARD) so that the variable will be cleaned up properly if one of them throws. Unfortunately, there's no way to express this properly in terms of nesting, as the regions for the temporaries overlap the region for the variable itself; if there are two temporaries, the variable needs to be the first thing destroyed if either of the temporary destructors throws. However, we only want to run the variable's cleanup if it actually got constructed. So we need to guard the temporary cleanups with the variable's cleanup if they are run on the normal path, but not if they are run on the exceptional path. We implement this by telling honor_protect_cleanup_actions to strip the variable cleanup from the exceptional path. Another approach could be to make the variable cleanup region enclose initialization, but depend on a flag to indicate that the variable is initialized; that's effectively what we do for arrays. But the current approach works fine for non-arrays, and has no code overhead in the usual case
